# Basics of hematology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Hematology and oncology > Basics of hematology and oncology > Basics of hematology*

[Original Article Link](/library/ln0vtg)

---

## Summary

Hematology is the study of blood and the disorders related to it. Human blood consists of blood cells and plasma. Blood has many functions, including transporting oxygen and <u>nutrients</u> to tissues, removing waste materials (e.g., carbon dioxide, <u>urea</u>), regulating body temperature, and carrying cells responsible for coagulation and <u>immune response</u>. There are three main types of blood cells, all of which originate from <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u>, which are located primarily in the <u>bone marrow</u>: <u>red blood cells</u> (<u>RBCs</u>; <u>erythrocytes</u>), <u>white blood cells</u> (<u>WBCs</u>; <u>leukocytes</u>), and <u>platelets</u> (<u>thrombocytes</u>). <u>RBCs</u> are <u>hemoglobin</u>-carrying cells that primarily transport oxygen. There are two types of <u>WBCs</u>: <u>granulocytes</u> and <u>lymphocytes</u>. <u>Granulocytes</u> are part of the <u>innate immune system</u> and play a key role in the <u>immune response</u> to bacteria, fungi, and <u>parasites</u>. <u>Lymphocytes</u> include cells that are responsible for both the innate (natural killers) and adaptive (T and <u>B cells</u>) <u>immune system</u>. T and <u>B cells</u>, in contrast to the cells involved in <u>innate immunity</u>, can target specific <u>antigens</u> presented to them by <u>antigen-presenting cells</u>. <u>Platelets</u>, small anucleate cells produced by <u>megakaryocytes</u>, are required for <u>hemostasis</u>.

---

## Overview

### Functions of blood [[1]](/library/Lvaw05)[[2]](/library/QHbuJE)




* Transport of:

* Oxygen, <u>nutrients</u>, and <u>hormones</u> to tissues

* Carbon dioxide to the <u>lungs</u> for elimination

* Metabolic waste products to <u>kidneys</u> and <u>liver</u> for elimination

* Protection from pathogens

* <u>Hemostasis</u>

* Regulation of body temperature, signal transmission, and acid-base <u>homeostasis</u>





### Blood volume




* On average, blood constitutes ∼ 7% of the total body weight of adults (∼ 70 mL/kg). [[1]](/library/Lvaw05)[[3]](/library/iHbJJE)

* The actual circulating blood volume varies and depends on age, weight, and height.

* For children ≥ 35 kg, <u>adolescents</u>, and adults, the total blood volume can be estimated using the Nadler equation: [[4]](/library/4Hb3qE)

* Men: BV = (0.3669 × H<sup>3</sup>) + (0.03219 × W) + 0.6041

* Women: BV = (0.3561 × H<sup>3</sup>) + (0.03308 × W) + 0.1833

* BV: blood volume in liters

* H: height in meters

* W: weight in kilograms

* For <u>neonates</u>, <u>infants</u>, and children up to 14 years, the following estimates can be used: [[5]](/library/PHbWqE)





| Blood volume in individuals of different age |  |
| --- | --- |
| Age | Estimated blood volume (mL/kg) |
| 0–30 days | 80–85 |
| 1–12 months | 75–80 |
| 13–24 months | 85 |
| 2–3 years | 80 |
| 4–6 years | 76–77 |
| 7–14 years | 70–75 |





### Blood constituents [[1]](/library/Lvaw05)[[2]](/library/QHbuJE)[[3]](/library/iHbJJE)




* Plasma: ∼ 55%

* The liquid constituent of blood

* Composed of water, <u>plasma proteins</u> (including <u>coagulation factors</u>), <u>electrolytes</u>, <u>hormones</u>, and other bioactive substances

* Blood cells: ∼ 45%

| Blood cells in peripheral tissue |  |  |  |  |
| <u>Macrophage</u> |  | <br><br>* Different in each tissue type (e.g., <u>Kupffer cells</u> in the <u>liver</u>, <u>histiocytes</u> in <u>connective tissue</u>)<br><br>* Activated by γ-<u>interferon</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Phagocytosis</u> of bacteria, senescent <u>RBCs</u>, and cellular debris<br><br>* <u>Antigen</u> presentation (<u>MHC II</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Mast cell</u> |  | <br><br>* Originates from <u>basophils</u><br><br>* <u>Basophilic</u> granules: <u>heparin</u>, <u>histamine</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Mediates <u>allergic reaction</u><br><br>* Binds <u>Fc</u> portion of <u>IgE</u> to membrane → <u>mast cell</u> <u>degranulation</u> → release of <u>histamine</u>, <u>heparin</u>, <u>tryptase</u>, and <u>eosinophil</u> <u>chemotactic</u> factors<br><br><br> |  |
| Dendritic cell |  | <br><br>* May derive from myeloid or lymphoid precursors [[6]](/library/hrYcSq)<br><br>* Expresses <u>MHC II</u> and <u>Fc receptor</u><br><br>* <u>Dendritic cells</u> in the <u>skin</u> are referred to as <u>Langerhans cells</u>.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Phagocytosis</u><br><br>* <u>Antigen-presenting cell</u> (<u>APC</u>)<br><br>* Links innate and <u>adaptive immune response</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Plasma cell</u> |  | <br><br>* Originates from <u>B lymphocytes</u><br><br>* Eccentric <u>nucleus</u><br><br>* <u>Chromatin</u> with clock face appearance<br><br>* Abundant <u>rough endoplasmic reticulum</u><br><br>* Well-developed <u>Golgi apparatus</u><br><br>* Does not circulate in peripheral blood<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Production of antibodies</u> specific to a particular <u>antigen</u><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas: Neutrophils > Lymphocytes > Monocytes > Eosinophils > Basophils.

## Bone marrow and hematopoiesis

### Bone marrow [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)[[7]](/library/LHbwIE)




* Definition

* Spongy, <u>soft tissue</u> that fills the hollow spaces within the <u>cancellous bone</u>

* Contains <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u> and stromal cells

* Function

* <u>Hematopoiesis</u> (main <u>function of bone</u> marrow)

* Filters <u>aging</u> <u>RBCs</u>

* Houses <u>immune cells</u> (e.g., <u>plasma cells</u>)





| <u>Types of bone</u> marrow |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Characteristic | Red marrow | Yellow marrow |
| Location | <br><br>* <u>Flat bones</u> (e.g., <u>sternum</u>, <u>skull</u>, <u>vertebrae</u>, <u>scapulae</u>, and <u>pelvic</u> bones)<br><br>* <u>Metaphysis</u> and <u>epiphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Shaft and <u>diaphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u> (e.g., <u>femur</u>, <u>tibia</u>, <u>humerus</u>)<br><br> |
| Function | <br><br>* <u>Hematopoiesis</u><br><br>* <u>Red marrow</u> gradually turns into <u>yellow marrow</u> with age.<br><br><br> | <br>* Not <u>hematopoietic</u> but can transform into <u>red marrow</u> (e.g., in chronic <u>hypoxia</u>, severe blood loss) [[8]](/library/h6YckJ)[[9]](/library/36YSkJ)<br><br> |
| <br>Composition <br> | <br><br>* <u>Hematopoietic</u> compartment<br><br>* <u>Hematopoietic stem cells</u> (organized in <u>hematopoietic</u> cords)<br><br>* Vascular compartment<br><br>* <u>Red marrow</u> is highly vascularized.<br><br>* Numerous sinusoids drain into a central longitudinal <u>vein</u>.<br><br>* Branches of <u>nutrient</u> <u>arteries</u> penetrate the bone cortex and enter the <u>medullary cavity</u> to provide blood supply to the <u>phagocyte</u>-lined venous spaces (sinusoids).<br><br>* Stroma: contains stromal cells (see below) and <u>reticular fibers</u> that support the <u>hematopoietic</u> compartment<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Fatty tissue</u> embedded within reticular stroma<br><br> |

#### Stromal cells of the bone marrow [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)[[7]](/library/LHbwIE)




Cells of the stromal compartment of <u>bone marrow</u> are not <u>hematopoietic</u> themselves, but they play a critical role in maintaining and regulating <u>hematopoiesis</u> (e.g., by removing potentially harmful cells and substances).




* Adventitial reticular cells

* Divide the <u>bone marrow</u> into islands of <u>hematopoietic</u> cells

* Accumulate fat: can transform <u>red marrow</u> into <u>yellow marrow</u>

* Mesenchymal stem cells

* <u>Pluripotent</u> <u>stem cells</u>

* Can differentiate into <u>macrophages</u>, <u>adipocytes</u>, <u>fibroblasts</u>, <u>osteoblasts</u>, <u>osteoclasts</u>, <u>chondrocytes</u>, <u>myocytes</u>, or <u>endothelial</u> cells

* Secrete stimulating factors required for <u>hematopoiesis</u>

* <u>Macrophages</u>:  : located around sinusoids, in the extravascular surface of the marrow





### Hematopoiesis (blood cell production) [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)




* Definition: <u>Hematopoiesis</u> is the process by which <u>multipotent</u> hematopoietic stem cells differentiate into either myeloid or lymphoid precursor cells and, eventually, into mature blood cells. ;  [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)

* Myeloid precursor cells develop into <u>erythrocytes</u>, <u>granulocytes</u>, or <u>megakaryocytes</u>.

* Lymphoid precursor cells develop into <u>lymphocytes</u> or <u>natural killer cells</u>

* <u>Hematopoietic</u> stem and progenitor cells express the <u>transmembrane protein</u> CD34 (used as a marker to identify and enrich <u>hematopoietic stem cells</u> in <u>bone marrow transplantation</u>). [[10]](/library/-WXDLC)

* <u>Dendritic cells</u> may derive from myeloid or lymphoid precursors. [[6]](/library/hrYcSq)

* Location

* Before <u>birth</u>: <u>yolk sac</u>, <u>spleen</u>, <u>liver</u>

* After <u>birth</u>

* <u>Bone marrow</u>

* Potentially <u>spleen</u> and <u>liver</u>, e.g., in the case of severe chronic <u>anemia</u> and some hematological malignancies (e.g., <u>Hodgkin lymphoma</u>)





![Hematopoiesis](media/t5wjmevfqmhvt64j3kaj5ba7.jpg)

Hematopoiesis




#### <u>Growth factors for hematopoiesis</u> [[1]](/library/Lvaw05)[[2]](/library/QHbuJE)




* <u>Hematopoietic growth factors</u> influence the differentiation and maturation of blood cells in all stages of their development.

* Some <u>interleukins</u> (e.g, <u>IL-3</u>, <u>IL-6</u>) also act as <u>hematopoietic growth factors</u>. See “<u>Cytokines and eicosanoids</u>” for more information.





| Overview of hematopoietic growth factors |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Growth factor | Produced by | Function |
| Stem cell factor(SCF) | <br>* <u>Stromal cells of the bone marrow</u><br><br> | <br>* Promotes <u>hematopoiesis</u><br><br> |
| <br><u>Granulocyte-monocyte colony-stimulating factor</u> (GM-CSF)<br> | <br>* <u>Endothelial</u> cells and <u>T cells</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Promotes <u>mitosis</u>, differentiation, and activity of <u>granulocyte</u>-<u>monocyte</u> <u>colony-forming units</u> (<u>CFU</u>-GM), <u>stem cells</u> that develop into <u>granulocytes</u> and <u>monocytes</u><br><br>* Therapeutic use: <u>sargramostim</u> (synthetic recombinant drug)<br><br>* Treatment of <u>neutropenia</u> following <u>chemotherapy</u> or <u>radiation therapy</u><br><br>* Myeloid reconstitution after <u>bone marrow transplantation</u><br><br>* Myelodysplasia<br><br>* <u>Aplastic anemia</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor</u> (G-CSF)<br> | <br>* <u>Endothelial</u> cells and <u>macrophages</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Promotes <u>mitosis</u>, differentiation, and activity of <u>granulocyte</u> <u>colony-forming units</u> (<u>CFU</u>-G), <u>stem cells</u> that develop into mature <u>granulocytes</u><br><br>* Promotes <u>neutrophil</u> activity<br><br>* Therapeutic use: <u>filgrastim</u> (synthetic recombinant drug)<br><br>* Treatment of <u>neutropenia</u> following <u>chemotherapy</u>, <u>radiation therapy</u>, or chronic <u>neutropenia</u><br><br>* Stimulates <u>granulocyte</u> precursors and thereby promotes <u>bone marrow</u> recovery and normalization of <u>WBC count</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Macrophage colony-stimulating factor</u> (M-CSF)<br> | <br>* <u>Endothelial</u> cells and <u>macrophages</u><br><br> | <br>* Promotes <u>mitosis</u>, differentiation, and activity of <u>monocyte</u> <u>colony-forming units</u> (<u>CFU</u>-M), <u>stem cells</u> that develop into <u>macrophages</u><br><br> |
| Erythropoietin (<u>EPO</u>) | <br>* <u>Fibroblast</u>-like <u>interstitial</u> cells surrounding the peritubular <u>capillaries</u> of the <u>kidneys</u> and <u>hepatocytes</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Promotes <u>erythropoiesis</u> in the <u>bone marrow</u> by stimulating <u>erythrocyte</u> <u>colony-forming units</u> (<u>CFU-E</u>)<br><br>* Therapeutic use: <u>recombinant EPO</u> analogs, e.g., <u>epoetin alfa</u><br><br>* Used to treat <u>anemia</u> (e.g., <u>anemia of chronic kidney disease</u>, <u>anemia</u> of <u>myelodysplastic syndromes</u>, <u>chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression</u>, <u>anemia</u> in individuals with <u>AIDS</u>)<br><br>* Can be abused to increase athletic performance (blood <u>doping</u>)<br><br>* Adverse effects: ↑ risk of <u>thromboembolism</u>; ↑ risk of <u>hypertension</u><br><br><br> |
| Thrombopoietin(<u>TPO</u>) | <br><br>* Mainly <u>parenchymal</u> cells and sinusoidal <u>endothelial</u> cells of the <u>liver</u><br><br>* Also <u>proximal convoluted tubule</u> cells of the <u>kidney</u> [[11]](/library/NKY-gJ)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Promotes <u>thrombopoiesis</u> by stimulating <u>megakaryocyte</u> <u>colony-forming units</u>, <u>stem cells</u> that give rise to <u>platelets</u><br><br>* Therapeutic use: used to stimulate <u>platelet production</u> to correct <u>low platelet count</u> (e.g., in autoimmune <u>thrombocytopenia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Romiplostim</u> (fusion protein analog)<br><br>* <u>Eltrombopag</u> (<u>thrombopoietin</u> <u>receptor</u> <u>agonist</u>)<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> RomiPLoSTIM STIMulates PLatelets. SarGRaMoSTIM STIMulates GRanulocytes and <u>Monocytes</u>.

## Red cell line: erythrocytes

### Erythropoiesis (<u>RBC</u> production) [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)




* Location

* During <u>embryogenesis</u>/<u>fetal development</u>

* Week 3–8: <u>yolk sac</u> [[12]](/library/mKYVSJ)

* Week 6–<u>birth</u>: <u>liver</u> [[12]](/library/mKYVSJ)

* Week 10–28: <u>spleen</u> [[13]](/library/5KYiSJ)

* After week 18: <u>red bone marrow</u> [[14]](/library/MKYMSJ)

* After <u>birth</u>: <u>red bone marrow</u>

* In children: <u>diaphyses</u> of <u>long bones</u> (e.g., <u>femur</u>, <u>tibia</u>)

* In adults: mainly plain bones (<u>pelvis</u>, <u>cranium</u>, <u>vertebrae</u>, <u>sternum</u>) and <u>metaphyses</u> of <u>long bones</u> [[15]](/library/nKY7SJ)

* Duration: approx. 1 week (production and maturation)

* Regulation: primarily <u>EPO</u>, along with other <u>hematopoietic growth factors</u>, including <u>GM-CSF</u>, <u>stem cell factor</u>, and <u>IL-3</u>

* Stages 

* In <u>bone marrow</u>
1. * <u>Hematopoietic stem cell</u> (erythroid progenitor cell)
2. * Proerythroblast: large cells with <u>basophilic</u> <u>cytoplasm</u> and a large <u>nucleus</u>
3. * Erythroblast: smaller <u>nucleus</u> than proerythroblasts; no nucleoli
4. * Normoblast: increasingly acidophilic <u>cytoplasm</u> with a compact <u>nucleus</u>
5. * Reticulocyte: acidophilic <u>cytoplasm</u> with granules composed of <u>cytoplasmic</u> <u>ribosomal RNA</u> (enabling <u>reticulocytes</u> to be stained with <u>methylene blue</u>)

* In blood
1. * <u>Reticulocytes</u> are released into the blood.
* The peripheral <u>reticulocyte count</u> reflects erythropoietic activity.

* Increased <u>reticulocytes</u> indicate increased <u>erythropoiesis</u> (e.g., due to <u>hemolysis</u>).

* <u>Decreased reticulocytes</u> indicate decreased <u>erythropoiesis</u> (e.g., due to <u>aplastic anemia</u>).
2. * After 1–2 days, <u>reticulocytes</u> mature into <u>erythrocytes</u>.

## White cell line: leukocytes

* <u>Leukocytes</u> are classified into two cell lines:

* Myeloid cell line: <u>granulocytes</u>, <u>mast cells</u>, and <u>monocytes</u>

* Lymphoid cell line: <u>lymphocytes</u>

* For more information on <u>WBC count</u> and its abnormalities, see “<u>Hematological parameters</u>” in “<u>Laboratory medicine</u>.”

## Myeloid cell line

### Myelopoiesis [[1]](/library/Lvaw05)[[2]](/library/QHbuJE)




* Definition: the process by which <u>granulocytes</u>, <u>monocytes</u>, and <u>mast cells</u> develop from myeloid precursor cells

* Location: <u>bone marrow</u>

* Duration: 6 days  [[16]](/library/6IYjdq)

* Stages of development

* <u>Granulocytes</u> (granulopoiesis) : <u>pluripotent</u> <u>hemopoietic</u> stem cell → common myeloid precursor cell → myeloblast → promyelocyte → eosinophilic, neutrophilic, or <u>basophilic</u> myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band cell → <u>granulocyte</u> (<u>eosinophil</u>/<u>neutrophil</u>/<u>basophil</u>)

* <u>Monocytes</u>: <u>pluripotent</u> <u>hemopoietic</u> stem cell → common myeloid precursor cell → <u>myeloblast</u> → monoblast → promonocyte → <u>monocyte</u>

* <u>Mast cells</u>: <u>pluripotent</u> <u>hemopoietic</u> stem cell → common myeloid precursor cell → <u>mast cell</u>

### Granulocytes [[1]](/library/Lvaw05)[[2]](/library/QHbuJE)[[17]](/library/wTahGP)[[18]](/library/q0YCSn)[[19]](/library/JsbsDE)




* <u>Granulocytes</u> make up the largest portion of <u>WBCs</u>: 1,500–8,500/mm<sup>3</sup>. [[20]](/library/IKYY3J)

* An increase (<u>granulocytosis</u>) or decrease (<u>granulocytopenia</u>; see “<u>Agranulocytosis</u>”) usually contributes the most to changes in the total <u>WBC count</u> (see “<u>Leukocytosis</u>” and “<u>Leukopenia</u>”).

* See also “<u>Hematological parameters</u>” in “<u>Laboratory medicine</u>.”





| Types of <u>granulocytes</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cell | Characteristics | Function | Causes of increase | Causes of decrease |
| <br>Neutrophil granulocyte   <br> | <br><br>* <u>Reference range</u>: 54–62% of all <u>leukocytes</u> in <u>WBC count</u><br><br>* Diameter: ∼ 12 μm<br><br>* <u>Half-life</u>: 6–8 hours [[16]](/library/6IYjdq)<br><br>* Maturation: Band neutrophils (immature) develop into segmented neutrophils (mature) over the course of 4–5 days.<br><br>* <u>5-HPETE</u>, <u>LTB4</u>, <u>IL-8</u>, <u>C5a</u>, <u>kallikrein</u>, and <u>platelet-activating factor</u> attract <u>neutrophils</u> to the site of inflammation.<br><br>* Inflammation results in:<br><br>* <u>Left shift</u><br><br>* Toxic granulation (coarse, dark blue granules located in the <u>cytoplasm</u>)<br><br>* Döhle bodies (light blue <u>cytoplasmic</u> <u>inclusions</u>)<br><br>* Toxic vacuolation<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Migrate to inflammation sites (<u>chemotaxis</u>)<br><br>* Identification, destruction, and <u>phagocytosis</u> of extracellular pathogens (e.g., bacteria, fungi)<br><br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Neutrophilia</u>.”<br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Neutropenia</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br>Eosinophil granulocyte <br> | <br><br>* <u>Reference range</u>: 1–3% of all <u>leukocytes</u><br><br>* Diameter: ∼ 12 μm<br><br>* <u>Half-life</u>: ∼ 1 hour [[16]](/library/6IYjdq)<br><br>* Eosinophilic (acidophile) granules<br><br>* Stain pink or red on H&E stain<br><br>* Contain <u>major basic protein</u> (<u>MBP</u>), histaminase, <u>eosinophil</u> peroxidase, <u>eosinophil</u> cationic protein, and <u>eosinophil</u>-derived <u>neurotoxin</u><br><br>* <u>Histamine</u>, <u>leukotrienes</u>, and <u>eosinophil</u> <u>chemotactic</u> factor, secreted by <u>mast cells</u>, attract <u>eosinophils</u> to the site of inflammation.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Immune response</u> to <u>parasites</u><br><br>* Migrate to inflammation sites (<u>chemotaxis</u>)<br><br>* Prevention of the spread of local inflammation<br><br>* Inactivation of proinflammatory substances (e.g., <u>histamine</u>, <u>leukotriene</u> C)<br><br>* <u>Phagocytosis</u> of <u>antigen-antibody complexes</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Eosinophilia</u>.”<br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Eosinopenia</u>.”<br><br> |
| <br>Basophil granulocyte <br> | <br><br>* <u>Reference range</u>: 0–0.75% of all <u>leukocytes</u><br><br>* Diameter: ∼ 10 μm<br><br>* <u>Half-life</u>: ∼ 6 hours [[16]](/library/6IYjdq)<br><br>* <u>Basophilic</u> granules<br><br>* Contain <u>histamine</u> and <u>heparin</u><br><br>* Often obscure the <u>nucleus</u><br><br>* Surface <u>receptors</u> for <u>IgE</u><br><br>* Remain in the bloodstream for minutes before migrating into tissue<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Production of leukotrienes→ inflammation and <u>allergic reaction</u><br><br>* Release of <u>histamine</u> and <u>heparin</u> → <u>vasodilation</u> and increased vessel permeability<br><br>* Almost no phagocytic abilities<br><br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Basophilia</u>.”<br><br> | <br>* Basopenia: difficult to assess because the normal <u>basophil</u> count is already very low<br><br> |

### <u>Monocytes</u>, <u>macrophages</u>, and <u>mast cells</u> [[1]](/library/Lvaw05)[[2]](/library/QHbuJE)[[21]](/library/u0Yp3n)][[22]](/library/v0YA3n)




| Characteristics of tissue-residing <u>immune cells</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cell type | Characteristics | Function | Causes of increase | Causes of decrease |
| Monocyte | <br><br>* 3–7% of all <u>leukocytes</u><br><br>* Diameter: ∼ 5–20 μm<br><br>* Remain in the bloodstream for only ∼ 8 hours before migrating to tissue<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Phagocytosis</u> and <u>antigen</u> presentation via <u>MHC I</u> and <u>MHC II</u> <u>receptors</u><br><br>* Migration into tissue → differentiation into <u>macrophages</u><br><br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Monocytosis</u>.”<br><br> | <br>* See “<u>Monocytopenia</u>.”<br><br> |
| Macrophage | <br><br>* <u>Monocytes</u> migrate to tissue and differentiate into <u>macrophages</u>.<br><br>* Surface <u>receptors</u><br><br>* <u>Fc receptors</u> (bind to the constant regions of <u>antibodies</u>)<br><br>* <u>Complement receptors</u> (e.g., C3b <u>receptors</u>)<br><br>* <u>Chemokine</u> <u>receptors</u> (e.g., <u>CCR5</u>, <u>CD40</u>)<br><br>* <u>Costimulation receptors</u> (e.g., <u>B7</u>)<br><br>* <u>Pattern recognition receptors</u> (e.g., <u>CD14</u> against <u>PAMP</u>)<br><br>* Tissue-specific subtypes <br><br>* <u>Osteoclasts</u> (bone)<br><br>* <u>Kupffer cells</u> (<u>liver</u>)<br><br>* <u>Microglia</u> (<u>brain</u> and spinal cord)<br><br>* <u>Histiocytes</u> (<u>connective tissue</u>)<br><br>* <u>Intraglomerular mesangial cells</u> (<u>kidneys</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Phagocytosis</u> of pathogens, foreign bodies, and dead cells  [[23]](/library/ksbmEE)<br><br>* <u>Antigen</u> presentation<br><br>* <u>Cytokine</u> production (e.g., TNF, <u>IL-1</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Present only in peripheral tissues; therefore, their concentration in the blood cannot be determined.<br><br>* For conditions characterized by dysfunctional <u>macrophages</u>, see “<u>Congenital neutrophil and phagocyte disorders</u>” in “<u>Congenital immunodeficiency disorders</u>.”<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Mast cell [[24]](/library/E0Y83n)<br> | <br><br>* Found in tissue (<u>interstitial connective tissue</u>, e.g., <u>submucosa</u> and surrounding <u>blood vessels</u>)<br><br>* Not present in the blood<br><br>* Contain <u>basophilic</u> granules and <u>receptors</u> for the <u>Fc</u> part of <u>IgE antibodies</u> (similarity to <u>basophils</u>)<br><br>* Express c-Kit <u>cell surface receptors</u><br><br>* Maturation occurs in target tissue.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>IgE</u> <u>antibodies</u> bind to <u>mast cell</u> surfaces → <u>allergen</u> contact triggers <u>degranulation</u> → <u>type 1 hypersensitivity</u> reaction<br><br>* Mutual stimulation of <u>basophils</u> and <u>eosinophils</u><br><br>* Nonimmunological <u>mast cell</u> <u>degranulation</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Systemic mastocytosis</u> (multiorgan involvement)<br><br>* <u>Cutaneous mastocytosis</u> (limited to <u>skin</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* N/A<br><br> |

## Lymphoid cell line

### Lymphopoiesis (<u>lymphocyte</u> production) [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)[[25]](/library/Bt0zf3)




* Stages of development: <u>pluripotent</u> <u>hematopoietic</u> stem cell → lymphoid progenitor cell → <u>T cell</u>, <u>B cell</u>, or <u>NK cell</u>

* Location of lymphopoiesis: initially in the <u>bone marrow</u>

* The location of maturation depends on <u>the cell</u> type.

* <u>T cells</u> mature in the <u>thymus</u>. See “<u>T cell development</u>.”

* <u>B cells</u> mature in the <u>bone marrow</u>.

* Mature <u>lymphocytes</u> migrate to <u>secondary lymphoid organs</u> (e.g., <u>lymph nodes</u>).

* <u>Lymphocyte</u> maturation

* During the <u>lymphocyte</u> lifecycle, several mechanisms ensure that T and <u>B cells</u> respond to a large variety of foreign <u>antigens</u>, while not reacting to self-<u>antigens</u>.
1. * Somatic recombination: Random recombination of <u>gene</u> segments coding for <u>lymphocyte</u> <u>receptors</u> enables a cell to specialize in responding to a specific <u>antigen</u>.
2. * <u>Central tolerance</u>: <u>apoptosis</u> induced in autoreactive cells (respond to self-<u>antigens</u>)
3. * Mature <u>lymphocytes</u> circulate through the bloodstream, migrate into tissue, and return to the blood via lymphatic vessels.
4. * <u>Peripheral tolerance</u>: Mature cells that respond to self-<u>antigens</u> become <u>anergic</u> (lose their function) or undergo <u>apoptosis</u>.

* For more detailed information about T- and <u>B-cell</u> maturation and selection, see “<u>Adaptive immune system</u>.”





### <u>Lymphocyte</u> physiology




* Concentration (blood)

* <u>Reference range</u>: 1,000–4,000/mm<sup>3</sup> or 25%–33% of total <u>leukocytes</u> [[19]](/library/JsbsDE)

* For causes of increase and decrease, see “<u>Lymphocytosis</u>” and “<u>Lymphopenia</u>.”

* Function

* <u>Humoral immune response</u> (<u>B cells</u>)

* <u>Cell-mediated immune response</u> (<u>T cells</u>, <u>natural killer cells</u>)

* <u>Immunological memory</u>

* See “<u>Adaptive immune system</u>” for more information.





### <u>T lymphocytes</u> (<u>T cells</u>)




* Function: part of the <u>acquired immune system</u>; see “<u>Adaptive immune system</u>”

* Surface markers

* All mature <u>T cells</u> express specific surface <u>proteins</u> that distinguish them from other <u>lymphocytes</u> and allow them to recognize <u>antigens</u> presented by <u>MHC</u> molecules of <u>antigen-presenting cells</u>.

* General <u>T-cell</u> markers: <u>CD3</u>, <u>CD28</u>, <u>TCR</u>

* The difference in surface protein expression (e.g., <u>CD4</u> vs. <u>CD8</u>) determines the specific function of <u>T-cell subtypes</u>.

* Subtypes: <u>T cells</u> can be largely divided into <u>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells</u> (<u>cytotoxic T cells</u>) and <u>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells</u> (<u>T helper cell</u> subpopulations). See “<u>T-cell subtypes</u>.”





#### CD4/CD8 ratio




* Definition: <u>CD4<sup>+</sup> T cell</u> levels divided by <u>CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell</u> levels

* Interpretation 

* ↑ <u>CD4/CD8 ratio</u> associated with:

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Crohn disease</u>

* Some <u>vasculitides</u> and <u>collagenases</u> (e.g., <u>granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>)

* ↓ <u>CD4/CD8 ratio</u> associated with:

* <u>HIV</u>

* <u>Extrinsic allergic alveolitis</u>





![image](media/uj86w4tq4oc08wxkeuhenv21.jpg)




#### Natural killer T cells (<u>NKT cells</u>) [[26]](/library/VaYGjn)




* Features

* Subtype of <u>T cells</u>

* Share characteristics of <u>NK cells</u> and <u>T cells</u>

* Have <u>T-cell receptors</u>

* Function

* Produce large amounts of immunomodulatory <u>cytokines</u> during infection or inflammation → modulate <u>immune response</u>

* Recognize <u>glycolipids</u> presented via CD1d





### <u>B lymphocytes</u> (<u>B cells</u>)




* Function: part of the <u>acquired immune system</u> (esp. <u>antibody production</u>); see “<u>Adaptive immune system</u>”

* Surface markers include:

* <u>CD20</u>

* <u>B-cell receptor</u> (<u>BCR</u>)

* Subtypes

* <u>Plasma cells</u>: After activation, <u>B cells</u> differentiate into <u>plasma cells</u>, which produce and secrete <u>antibodies</u>.

* <u>Memory B cells</u>: specialized <u>plasma cells</u> that provide a fast and specific <u>immune response</u> to reexposure to <u>antigens</u>





### Natural killer cells (<u>NK cells</u>) [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)[[27]](/library/XJ09sS)[[28]](/library/GgaB9P)




* Function

* Part of the <u>innate immune system</u> [[29]](/library/hEYcvI)

* Detection and destruction of:

* <u>Tumor</u> cells

* Cells infected with <u>viruses</u> (esp. <u>HHV</u> family)

* Physiology

* Can arise from both lymphoid and myeloid precursor cells [[29]](/library/hEYcvI)

* Surface markers

* Fc receptor (CD16): a <u>membrane receptor</u> protein that recognizes and binds to <u>antibodies</u> that have attached to pathogens

* Mediates a phagocytic and/or cytotoxic response

* Found on many <u>immune cells</u>, e.g., <u>NK cells</u>, <u>neutrophils</u>, and <u>macrophages</u>

* CD56: a neural <u>cell adhesion molecule</u> specific to <u>NK cells</u>

* Produce <u>IFN-γ</u> and <u>TNF-α</u> (<u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> that recruit <u>macrophages</u> and promote <u>phagocytosis</u>)

* Stimulated by <u>IFN-α</u>, <u>IFN‑β</u>, <u>IL-2</u>, and <u>IL-12</u>

* Mechanism of action

* <u>NK cells</u> are activated under the following conditions:

* Nonspecific activation by a signal from a hostile cell (e.g., lipid <u>antigens</u> that are copresented with CD1 molecule)

* Absence of <u>MHC I</u> <u>receptors</u> on the hostile cell (e.g., virally infected cells that do not express <u>MHC I</u> due to downregulation)

* Mechanisms for <u>pathogen</u> elimination

* Induction of <u>apoptosis</u>, e.g., via the following enzymes:

* Granzyme: a <u>serine</u> <u>protease</u> secreted by <u>NK cells</u> and <u>cytotoxic T cells</u>

* Perforin: a pore-forming protein secreted by <u>NK cells</u> and <u>cytotoxic T cells</u>

* <u>Perforin</u> forms a pore for <u>granzyme B</u> to enter the <u>target cell</u>

* <u>Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity</u> (activated by CD16-binding <u>Fc region</u> of bound <u>IgG</u>)

## Platelets

### Thrombopoiesis (<u>platelet production</u>) [[2]](/library/QHbuJE)




* Location: <u>bone marrow</u>

* Duration: ∼ 1 week for production and maturation

* Regulation: <u>thrombopoietin</u>

* Secreted by <u>liver</u> and <u>kidneys</u>

* Stimulates megakaryocyte <u>proliferation</u> and maturation in <u>bone marrow</u> (megakaryopoiesis)

* Stages of <u>thrombopoiesis</u>: myeloid precursor cell → megakaryoblasts → <u>megakaryocytes</u>  → <u>platelets</u>





![Megakaryocyte](media/uu75r6884rbvfb9uwp06q39h.jpg)

Megakaryocyte




### <u>Platelet</u> physiology




* Lifespan: 8–10 days

* Concentration

* <u>Reference range</u>: 150,000–400,000/mm<sup>3</sup>

* The <u>spleen</u> stores about a third of the body's <u>platelets</u>, and these are not included in the <u>platelet count</u>.

* Abnormal <u>platelet count</u>: See “<u>Thrombocytosis</u>” and “<u>Thrombocytopenia</u>.”

* Function: <u>primary hemostasis</u> [[30]](/library/A0YRin)

* <u>Platelet</u> granules

* Dense granules: <u>ADP</u>, <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u>, <u>serotonin</u>, <u>histamine</u>

* Alpha granules: <u>vWF</u>, <u>fibrinogen</u>, <u>fibronectin</u>, <u>platelet</u> factor 4
